Understanding road safety across Great Britain

Key findings

What the data says

Four headline results from the full 2005–2017 accident file.

−34.6%

Steady long-term decline

Recorded accidents fell from 198,735 in 2005 to 129,982 in 2017.

17:00

Evening rush is the peak

181,881 records at 17:00, with a second peak at 08:00. Friday and November lead their categories.

74.6%

Single carriageways dominate

Most records occur on single carriageways, though counts are not adjusted for road length or traffic.

15.3%

Most accidents are slight

Of known-severity records, 1.3% are fatal and 14.0% serious. The rest are slight.

Methodology

A reproducible big-data workflow

From raw Kaggle CSVs to tested findings, using Spark for scale and compact summaries for visualisation.

Ingest

Read 673 MB accident and 615 MB vehicle CSVs in Spark.

Validate

Check keys, grain, missing values and year coverage.

Clean

Normalise missing markers and engineer date, hour and severity fields.

Explore

Time, conditions, location, vehicles and drivers.

Test

Spearman correlation and chi-square with effect sizes.

Model

Class-weighted logistic regression baseline.

Results

Statistical tests and model

Associations are statistically significant but small, and the baseline model has limited predictive power.

Chi-square tests with severity

1,436weather χ²
569road surface χ²
0.019Cramér’s V, weather
0.012Cramér’s V, surface
  • Both p-values are far below 0.05.
  • With millions of rows, tiny effects become significant, so effect size matters more.

Severity classifier (Fatal/Serious vs Slight)

0.623ROC-AUC
0.222PR-AUC
0.646weighted F1
60%severe-class recall
  • Casualty count is excluded to avoid target leakage.
  • Severe-class precision is only 0.21: an academic baseline, not an operational tool.
Interpret with care

Limitations and next steps

Record counts, severity shares, vehicle involvements and exposure-adjusted risk answer different questions.

What this analysis cannot establish

  • Licence status: neither file has that field.
  • Risk per mile, trip or driver: no exposure data.
  • Causation from correlations, tests or model coefficients.
  • Risk rankings from raw district, vehicle, sex or age counts.
  • Full vehicle linkage in the Kaggle extract.

Recommended follow-up

  • Add traffic-flow or vehicle-mile data to compute rates.
  • Use the casualty-level file for injury severity by road user.
  • Refresh with current DfT data and document coding changes.
  • Check missingness and linkage by year before comparing vehicles.
  • Validate and calibrate before any operational use.
